Crawl. A bizarre local co-op dungeon crawler where you murder your friends and then haunt them as a ghost that takes control of monsters.

This has been sitting in my library unplayed for who knows how long, but damn. This game is actually fun. Essentially the premise is that at any point during the game only one of the up to 4 players may be alive and playing the hero. The other three will be ghosts with the ability to inhabit monsters and other various traps found in the rooms. It becomes their job to kill the live player who is trying to complete the dungeon. The ghost that successfully does this becomes the live player, and the crawl continues.

The pixel art graphics are a bit terrible, but if you can get past that this is a winner. It has no online play at all, so make sure you invite your victims .. err, friends over.

I go through phases of this. I definitely notice newer games continually fail to grab my interest like they used to. I'm not sure what it is.

Part of me wants to blame newer games for being fundamentally different. They mostly amount to multi-player only experiences, giant sandboxes with a tacked on goal, or just pure sandboxes with no goals what so ever. They are all constantly under development, so in a constant state of flux. I never feel like I've really mastered a game, because it's constantly changing out from under me. Plus, the fact that they are so open ended just feels daunting. I have limited time for games. I grew up with games that told me when they were over and I could move on. Now they expect me to decide that for myself. I don't like it.

I increasingly find myself going back to older games from the 00's, 90's or even 80's. I beat Curse of the Azure Bonds recently, and loved it. I'm working on Baldur's Gate and enjoying that greatly as well.

This wraps up one aspect of my feelings toward games. Too sandboxed and completing missions/quests felt a bit more like a progression chore then actually making progress in a game. I feel Morrowind and Skyrim are a perfect example of this. Morrowind GOTY had a lot more story/substance than Skyrim will all its DLC ever had in my opinion.

Yeah, almost nothing you do in an Elder Scrolls game has any impact.

Then I think back to my time in Fallout 1 & 2. Every town I visited I frequently left fundamentally changed. I'd roll into town, upend the entire power structure, take down gangs, re-unite families, discover prewar artifacts. That was a game where your impact on the world really drove you on.

Yeah Interplay's games were great in that you actually made an impact on the world you were playing in hell other games from that era were great as well. Too bad devs are straying more far from this formula in favor in more cookie cutter approaches.

Maybe you should try being more selective of the games you play, after all the number of games that come out each year at this point is far beyond what anyone can actual get through. Personally I've had it with most AAA titles, they are more about money than the art form (Naughty Dog is an exception) and that applies to Fallout 4 tbh, that wasn't the case with the older games you keep going back to. Some of my favorite recent games have been indie titles, and that doesn't necessarily mean they are just retro style games. Two I'll recommend are Ori and the Blind Forest, and Transistor, both really original and a testament to the craft. Ya gotta do some diggin dude, the modern gaming industry is just like the music industry in that you often have to look past the mass marketed crap to find the true artists.
